name: JFE150DCKR
title: JFE150: N-channel JFET for ultra-low-noise audio and sensor inputs, with gate clamp diodes, in SC70 and SOT-23
summary: The JFE150 is a single N-channel depletion JFET for very quiet, very high-impedance input stages such as microphone, hydrophone and piezoelectric preamplifiers. Biased at 5 mA its input-referred voltage noise is 0.8 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz, with gate leakage of 10 pA maximum and 24 pF input capacitance at VDS = 5 V. Two extra pins, VCH and VCL, give the gate its own clamp diodes to an upper and a lower rail; both are left open when no clamping is needed. It comes in a 5-pin SC70 (DCK) or SOT-23 (DBV); JFE150DCKR is the SC70 on a 3000-piece reel.

pins.name: VCH
pins.function: Upper clamp node. A diode inside conducts from the gate to this pin when the gate rises above it. Leave it open when no clamping is wanted.

pins.name: VCL
pins.function: Lower clamp node. A diode inside conducts from this pin to the gate when the gate falls below it. Leave it open when no clamping is wanted. It sits where the gate pin of an older three-lead JFET sits.

circuits.title: Noise measurement circuit
circuits.description: The common-source stage used to measure the noise figures. RD = 10 kΩ loads the drain from V+, and RS = 10 kΩ returns the source to V-, bypassed to ground by 3 mF. V- is trimmed to set IDS, then V+ is trimmed to set VDS. The drain signal is ac-coupled through 1 µF into an OPA210 wired as a non-inverting amplifier with 10 kΩ feedback and 100 Ω to ground, with 100 kΩ biasing its input to ground and 49.9 Ω in series with its output. The gain from VIN to VOUT is measured and used to refer the output noise back to the gate.
notes: VCH and VCL are open. The op amp's supply pins are not given.

circuits.title: Gate clamp in a phantom-powered microphone input
circuits.description: A 48 V phantom supply feeds the microphone line through 6.8 kΩ, and CDC (10 µF) couples the line to the gate through RG, with RB setting the gate's dc level. With the microphone unplugged CDC charges to 48 V; if the line is next shorted (the switch), the gate voltage can pass its VGS rating. The clamp then conducts: the discharge current iG runs between the gate and VCL, which returns to ground through RL, and RG with RL limits that current while the clamp holds the gate at a safe level. RG's thermal noise reaches the gate directly, so it is kept small. The drain and source loads go to rails the circuit leaves unnamed.

parts.note: stands for the microphone line being shorted to ground
polarised, positive side toward the line

notes: SW1 is a changeover: pin C is the common, A the throw to the phantom feed, B the throw to ground. RG, RB, RL and the drain and source loads carry no values.

circuits.title: Common-source amplifier
circuits.description: The basic open-loop gain stage: the input drives the gate through RG, RS from source to ground sets the bias current together with the JFET's threshold, and RD from V+ is the drain load where the output is taken. The gain is Equation 1; it rises with bias current because gm does.
notes: No values are given. VCH and VCL are open.

circuits.title: Common-source amplifier with current-source biasing
circuits.description: The same stage with the source resistor replaced by a current sink IBIAS to V-. The bias current no longer depends on the JFET's threshold voltage, and because the sink has a high output impedance a smaller bypass capacitor CS from source to ground gives the same filtering.
notes: No values are given. VCH and VCL are open.

circuits.title: Composite amplifier, JFET front end with op amp
circuits.description: Composite amplifier using current feedback. The JFET is a common-source stage (RD, RS) whose drain is ac-coupled by CD into the inverting input of an op amp, whose non-inverting input sits at a bias VBIASO. The op amp's output feeds back through RF2 into the JFET source, where RS2 in series with CS returns it to ground for ac, so the closed-loop gain is RF2 / RS2 (Equation 4) rather than the JFET's spread of gm. RF and CF close the op amp's own loop and set its corner (Equation 3). CB couples VIN to the gate and RB biases the gate; RG is in series with the gate. The JFET adds open-loop gain ahead of the op amp, widening the bandwidth and giving a quiet, high-impedance input.
notes: No values are given; Table 9-1 gives each part's role. RB returns to a rail the circuit leaves unnamed. VCH and VCL are not connected, and the op amp's supply pins are not shown.

circuits.title: Low-noise, high-input-impedance composite amplifier (typical application)
circuits.description: The composite amplifier with values, built for 60 dB of gain from 60 Hz to 20 kHz with under 1.5 nV/√Hz of noise and under 100 pA of input current. The JFET runs from 12 V with RD = 10 kΩ and RS = 300 Ω; the input is coupled by 10 µF, biased to ground by 1 MΩ and fed through 10 Ω. The drain is coupled by 10 µF into an OPA202 whose non-inverting input sits at 6 V, so in closed loop the drain also settles at 6 V. RF2 = 10 kΩ over RS2 = 10 Ω sets the gain of 1000; 470 µF in series with RS2 keeps the feedback from shifting the bias. 1 MΩ with 10 pF closes the op amp's local loop. Figures 9-7 and 9-8 show the measured gain and noise.
notes: VCH and VCL are open. The op amp's supply pins are not given.

circuits.description: The connections of the common-source layout: VCH tied to VDD and VCL to VSS so the clamp diodes are active, RD from VDD to the drain, RS with CS in parallel from the source to VSS, and the input to the gate.

operation.text: An N-channel depletion JFET built on a modern analog bipolar process, aimed at low-noise gain stages behind sources of very high impedance: piezoelectric sensors, transducers, large condenser microphones and hydrophones. Its process gives tighter parameter control than an ordinary discrete JFET, a high ratio of gm to CISS, and very low gate current.

Flicker (1/f) noise governs systems that need gain below 100 Hz, and this part keeps it very low. Above 1 kHz the noise is thermal and set by gm, which follows the drain bias current, so the thermal noise also follows the bias current (Figures 6-4, 6-9, 6-11). The noise figures were taken with the circuit of Figure 7-1.

Input current noise is the shot noise of the gate current, so with gate current this small it is almost always negligible; for a resistive source the source's own thermal noise dominates long before current noise matters (Figure 6-10).
Gate current is 10 pA maximum at room temperature. As in any JFET it grows with drain-to-source voltage (Figure 6-5); holding VDS under 5 V gives the lowest gate current.

Low-leakage diodes inside the package connect the gate to VCH (conducting when the gate rises above VCH) and to VCL (conducting when the gate falls below VCL), so surges and ESD on the input are steered away from the gate without external diodes, whose leakage and nonlinear capacitance would add distortion. Further diodes run from the drain and the source to the clamp pins. The diodes take 200 mA for 50 ms but no more than 20 mA continuously. They are optional: the gate tolerates -40 V, so if the input stays inside that, leave VCH and VCL open.

On older three-lead JFETs the gate sits in the position of the JFE150's pin 2 (VCL). To try the part in such a socket, short pin 2 to pin 3 (G). That shorts out the lower clamp diode, so it no longer protects, and adds about 1 pF to CISS (Figure 6-12).

Piezoelectric transducers have output impedances above 10 MΩ and need a very high impedance load. With IG at most ±10 pA and CISS of 24 pF the part suits transducers of more than 240 pF; on a smaller transducer, CISS divides down the signal and the noise performance suffers.

With VGS below VGSC the channel is shut and only junction leakage flows. Above VGSC, a VDS below the linear-to-saturation threshold (Figure 8-1) puts the part in the linear region, where it acts as a drain-to-source resistance that VGS changes little; above the threshold it is in saturation, where IDS follows VGS through gm.

In Figure 9-2, IDS is fixed jointly by RS and the JFET's threshold voltage VT (Figure 9-3 gives IDS against RS at VDS = 5 V). The bias therefore moves with resistor and threshold tolerance, and RS's thermal noise appears in the output. A current source in place of RS (Figure 9-4) removes the threshold from the bias and lets a smaller CS do the same filtering.

Placing the JFET ahead of an op amp (Figures 9-5, 9-6) gives a gain fixed by resistors instead of by the JFET's transconductance, which varies widely; the JFET stage adds open-loop gain, extending bandwidth beyond the op amp alone, and gives a high-impedance, very quiet input for high-impedance microphones.

First choose the bias current from the noise you need (Figure 6-11) and set it with RS (Figure 9-3); bias current and stage gain dominate the input noise. Then make RD as large as possible while keeping at least 2 V from drain to source, so the JFET never enters its linear region; in closed loop the op amp holds the drain at its non-inverting input's voltage, and normally only this dc point matters since the drain's ac swing is small. Set the closed-loop gain with RF2 and RS2 (Equation 4), keeping RS2 small since its thermal noise enters directly. CS keeps the feedback's dc from moving the bias set by RS and forms the low-frequency roll-off (Equation 5).
The part has no supply pins. With system rails of 40 V or more, check every pin against its absolute maximum voltage.

Run input traces well apart from supply and output traces, crossing them at right angles if they must cross. Keep input traces short and high-impedance inputs away from noisy traces; the input is the most sensitive node. Place parts close to the device, keeping the source and drain components especially close, and filter the supplies well. Guarding the gate traces with a ring driven from a low impedance cuts leakage from nearby traces at other voltages. Clean the board after assembly; after any aqueous wash, bake it, for example at 85 °C for 30 minutes, to drive moisture out of the package. Figure 9-9 shows a common-source layout: VCH tied to VDD, VCL to VSS, RD from VDD to the drain, RS and CS in parallel from the source to VSS, and the input to the gate.
